pages.text: On Saturday morning at Uncle Ofori’s vegetable farm near Dawhenya on the Accra Plains, eleven-year-old Kojo and his friend Ama crouched beside an open plot of tomato plants. Yesterday’s heavy rainstorm had knocked yellow blossoms into the mud, and tiny whiteflies buzzed under curling leaves. ‘Farming outdoors is tough!’ sighed Kojo.
sentences: On Saturday morning at Uncle Ofori’s vegetable farm near Dawhenya on the Accra Plains, eleven-year-old Kojo and his friend Ama crouched beside an open plot of tomato plants.
Yesterday’s heavy rainstorm had knocked yellow blossoms into the mud, and tiny whiteflies buzzed under curling leaves.
‘Farming outdoors is tough!’ sighed Kojo.
pages.alt: Kojo and Ama crouch with Uncle Ofori beside an outdoor tomato bed where rain has splashed mud onto drooping leaves.

pages.text: Uncle Ofori smiled and pointed across the yard to a tall, arched structure covered with clear UV-protected roof film and fine white mesh netting along the sides. ‘That is why we are testing controlled-environment farming,’ he said. ‘Welcome to our tropical greenhouse! Let us step through the double-door entry and wash our boots in the disinfectant tray.’

‘That is why we are testing controlled-environment farming,’ he said.

pages.alt: Uncle Ofori leads Kojo and Ama toward a bright arched tropical greenhouse with mesh side walls and a double-door entrance.

pages.text: Inside the greenhouse, neat rows of tall tomato vines climbed up strings, heavy with clusters of smooth red and green tomatoes! ‘Look how healthy the leaves are!’ said Ama. ‘How does a greenhouse work, Uncle Ofori?’ ‘First,’ he explained, ‘the clear roof lets sunlight shine through so the green leaves can perform photosynthesis, using light, water and carbon dioxide to make sugars for the fruit.’
sentences: Inside the greenhouse, neat rows of tall tomato vines climbed up strings, heavy with clusters of smooth red and green tomatoes!
‘Look how healthy the leaves are!’ said Ama.

‘How does a greenhouse work, Uncle Ofori?’ ‘First,’ he explained, ‘the clear roof lets sunlight shine through so the green leaves can perform photosynthesis, using light, water and carbon dioxide to make sugars for the fruit.’
pages.alt: Inside the sunlit greenhouse, healthy tomato vines climb vertical strings heavy with red and green tomatoes.

pages.text: ‘At the same time,’ Uncle Ofori continued, ‘the roof shields the delicate tomato flowers from pounding rainstorms that bruise fruit and splash soil fungi onto the leaves. And because the roof and walls enclose the space, warm air stays inside instead of blowing away on the wind.’
sentences: ‘At the same time,’ Uncle Ofori continued, ‘the roof shields the delicate tomato flowers from pounding rainstorms that bruise fruit and splash soil fungi onto the leaves.
And because the roof and walls enclose the space, warm air stays inside instead of blowing away on the wind.’
pages.alt: Uncle Ofori points to the curved roof sheltering yellow tomato blossoms from outdoor wind and rain.

pages.text: Kojo raised his pencil. ‘Uncle, in science class we heard about the atmospheric greenhouse effect warming the whole Earth. Is that the exact same thing as this farm greenhouse?’ ‘Great question, Kojo!’ said Uncle Ofori. ‘They share a name, but they work differently. A farm greenhouse stays warm mainly because its solid roof and walls physically stop warm air from rising and blowing away.’
sentences: Kojo raised his pencil.
‘Uncle, in science class we heard about the atmospheric greenhouse effect warming the whole Earth.
Is that the exact same thing as this farm greenhouse?’ ‘Great question, Kojo!’ said Uncle Ofori.
‘They share a name, but they work differently.
A farm greenhouse stays warm mainly because its solid roof and walls physically stop warm air from rising and blowing away.’
pages.alt: Kojo holds his clipboard and asks Uncle Ofori about the difference between a farm greenhouse and Earth’s atmosphere.

pages.text: ‘In Earth’s atmosphere,’ Uncle Ofori explained, ‘there is no plastic roof in the sky! Instead, gases like carbon dioxide, water vapour and methane absorb invisible heat radiation rising from the ground and send some of it back toward Earth. So our farm greenhouse is a physical shelter for plants, whereas the atmospheric greenhouse effect is about heat-absorbing gases around the planet.’

Instead, gases like carbon dioxide, water vapour and methane absorb invisible heat radiation rising from the ground and send some of it back toward Earth.
So our farm greenhouse is a physical shelter for plants, whereas the atmospheric greenhouse effect is about heat-absorbing gases around the planet.’
pages.alt: Uncle Ofori shows a sketch comparing a roofed farm greenhouse with Earth surrounded by heat-absorbing gases.

pages.text: Ama looked at a thermometer hanging at plant height: it read twenty-eight degrees Celsius. ‘Wait,’ she said, ‘in hot Ghanaian sunshine, wouldn’t a closed plastic box get far too hot inside?’ ‘Exactly right!’ said Uncle Ofori. ‘If a greenhouse has poor ventilation in our tropical climate, temperatures can shoot above thirty-eight degrees, spoiling tomato pollen and wilting the crop!’
sentences: Ama looked at a thermometer hanging at plant height: it read twenty-eight degrees Celsius.
‘Wait,’ she said, ‘in hot Ghanaian sunshine, wouldn’t a closed plastic box get far too hot inside?’ ‘Exactly right!’ said Uncle Ofori.
‘If a greenhouse has poor ventilation in our tropical climate, temperatures can shoot above thirty-eight degrees, spoiling tomato pollen and wilting the crop!’
pages.alt: Ama checks a hanging thermometer while Uncle Ofori points to the high roof vents and breathable mesh walls.

pages.text: ‘That is why tropical greenhouses in Ghana are designed with high roof vents and roll-up side walls covered with fine mesh,’ Uncle Ofori showed them. ‘Hot air rises and escapes out of the top vent while cooler air flows in through the sides. We also watch humidity carefully: if the air stays too damp without airflow, mould and fungi can attack the leaves.’
sentences: ‘That is why tropical greenhouses in Ghana are designed with high roof vents and roll-up side walls covered with fine mesh,’ Uncle Ofori showed them.
‘Hot air rises and escapes out of the top vent while cooler air flows in through the sides.
We also watch humidity carefully: if the air stays too damp without airflow, mould and fungi can attack the leaves.’
pages.alt: Gentle airflow arrows in the sunlit space show hot air rising out of the roof vent while fresh air enters through the side netting.

pages.text: Kojo knelt by the base of a plant where a thin black tube released slow, steady drops of water right at the roots. ‘Why don’t you spray water over the whole room with a hose?’ he asked. ‘This is drip irrigation,’ said Uncle Ofori. ‘Greenhouses still need plenty of clean water, Kojo, but drip lines deliver measured water and plant nutrients straight to the roots. Less water evaporates into the air, and the leaves stay dry and healthy!’

‘This is drip irrigation,’ said Uncle Ofori.
‘Greenhouses still need plenty of clean water, Kojo, but drip lines deliver measured water and plant nutrients straight to the roots.
Less water evaporates into the air, and the leaves stay dry and healthy!’
pages.alt: Kojo kneels beside a black drip-irrigation tube releasing small drops of water directly at the base of a tomato stem.

pages.text: ‘And what about the whiteflies we saw outside?’ asked Ama, pointing to a small yellow sticky card hanging near the door. ‘The fine side netting blocks most insects from flying in,’ said Uncle Ofori, ‘so we spray far less pesticide. However, a greenhouse never eliminates all pests by magic! Tiny pests can still sneak in on clothes or tools. That is why we use yellow sticky traps to monitor insects and inspect every row each morning.’

Tiny pests can still sneak in on clothes or tools.
That is why we use yellow sticky traps to monitor insects and inspect every row each morning.’
pages.alt: Ama and Uncle Ofori inspect a yellow sticky pest-monitoring card hanging near the greenhouse entrance.

pages.text: At the farm table, Uncle Ofori opened his account book. ‘Does a greenhouse guarantee easy money?’ he asked. ‘No! Building the frame, replacing torn nets, pumping water and buying quality seeds all cost money. This season, our seeds and compost cost three hundred cedis, water and nutrients cost two hundred and fifty cedis, labour and routine maintenance cost two hundred and fifty cedis, and our net-and-frame upkeep cost two hundred cedis. That is one thousand cedis in total costs.’

This season, our seeds and compost cost three hundred cedis, water and nutrients cost two hundred and fifty cedis, labour and routine maintenance cost two hundred and fifty cedis, and our net-and-frame upkeep cost two hundred cedis.
That is one thousand cedis in total costs.’
pages.alt: At a wooden table outside the greenhouse, Uncle Ofori reviews his farm budget notebook with Kojo and Ama.

pages.text: Kojo calculated quickly on his clipboard. ‘We harvested eighty crates of firm, clean tomatoes and sold them at twenty cedis per crate. Eighty times twenty is one thousand six hundred cedis in sales! Subtracting the one thousand cedis of costs leaves six hundred cedis of real profit!’ Uncle Ofori beamed. ‘When science, careful ventilation and honest budgeting work together, smart farming can feed Ghana’s future!’ The end.

activities.question: How does a farm greenhouse structure differ from Earth’s atmospheric greenhouse effect?
options: A farm greenhouse traps air with a roof; the atmosphere uses gases
Earth has a giant plastic sheet floating in space above the clouds
A farm greenhouse works without any sunlight at all
There is no difference; both are made of wooden poles and netting
activities.explanation: A farm greenhouse physically encloses air with a roof and walls, whereas the atmospheric greenhouse effect involves gases absorbing and re-emitting infrared heat.

activities.question: What happens in a Ghanaian greenhouse if it has poor ventilation on a hot day?
options: It overheats above 38 °C and traps damp air, harming pollen and leaves
It turns into a freezer and covers the tomatoes in snow
The plants grow ten times faster without needing any water
activities.explanation: Without roof vents and mesh airflow, tropical greenhouses overheat quickly and high humidity promotes fungal diseases.

activities.definition: Supplying water to crops through pipes, channels or drip lines to help them grow.
distractors: Cutting down old tomato vines after harvest
Selling crates of vegetables at the market

activities.question: Uncle Ofori sold 80 crates at 20 cedis each (1,600 cedis) and spent 1,000 cedis on costs. What was his profit?
activities.explanation: Revenue (80 × 20 = 1,600 cedis) minus Total Costs (300 + 250 + 250 + 200 = 1,000 cedis) equals 600 cedis profit.

activities.prompt: Why must greenhouse farmers still wash their boots and check yellow sticky traps even when insect netting covers the walls?
Put the steps of Uncle Ofori’s greenhouse management in order.
items: Wash boots at the double-door entry to keep soil pests out.
Use roof vents and mesh walls to keep temperature around 28 °C.
Deliver water and nutrients straight to roots with drip irrigation.
Record all 1,000 cedis of costs and subtract from 1,600 cedis of sales.

activities.prompt: How do you feel when you see how science, hard work and careful maths can help farmers grow healthy food in Ghana?

The movement of fresh air through a space to control heat and dampness.
The amount of invisible water vapour held in the air.
A system for supplying measured water to farm crops; drip irrigation waters the roots directly.
The money left over from sales after every business cost has been subtracted.
